L0@P0: SENATE JUDICIARY COMMITTEE
L1@P0: Senator Thomas Umberg, Chair
L2@P0: 2023-2024 Regular Session
L3@P0: AB 2835 (Gabriel)
L4@P0: Version: June 3, 2024
L5@P0: Hearing Date: June 11, 2024
L6@P0: Fiscal: Yes
L7@P0: Urgency: No
L8@P0: ID
L9@P0: SUBJECT
L10@P0: Motels and hotels: publicly funded shelter programs
L11@P0: DIGEST
L12@P0: This bill eliminates the sunset date of January 1, 2025 on the tenancy rules and the
L13@P0: exception to standard landlord-tenant rules for interim homeless shelter programs by
L14@P0: participating hotels or motels.
L15@P0: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
L16@P0: California is experiencing a severe affordable housing and homelessness crisis. In 2023,
L17@P0: more than 181,000 individuals were estimated to be experiencing homelessness in the
L18@P0: state, 68 percent of whom were living outside without access to temporary shelter. One
L19@P0: of the ways California has attempted to address this crisis is by utilizing hotels and
L20@P0: motels as temporary shelters for those experiencing homelessness. Project Roomkey
L21@P0: was created during the COVID-19 pandemic to do just that. However, hotels and motels
L22@P0: have either been hesitant to participate in such shelter programs because of the
L23@P0: possibility that program participants who reside in the shelter for more than 30 days
L24@P0: may become entitled to standard landlord-tenant protections. There were reports as
L25@P0: well that participating hotels and motels were engaging in the practice of “shuffling’
L26@P0: program participants, forcing participants to move before they reach the 30 day mark
L27@P0: and assume landlord-tenant protections, in order to avoid needing to comply with
L28@P0: landlord-tenant laws when program participants are removed from the program. To
L29@P0: resolve this issue, the Legislature enacted AB 1991 to specifically exempt residents of
L30@P0: hotel or motel shelter programs from landlord-tenant laws and establish a separate set
L31@P0: of standards for the removal of residents in such shelter programs. The provisions
L32@P0: created by AB 1991 are set to expire January 1, 2025. AB 2835 proposes to eliminate this
L33@P0: sunset provision, making the program and its exemptions from landlord-tenant law
L34@P0: permanent. AB 1991 is sponsored by the National Alliance to End Homelessness and
L35@P0-1: Los Angeles Family Housing, and is supported by a number of pro-housing and antihomelessness organizations. The Committee has received no timely opposition.AB 2835 (Gabriel)
L36@P1: Page 2 of 10
L37@P1: PROPOSED CHANGES TO THE LAW
L38@P1: Existing law:
L39@P1: 1) Defines “motel or hotel” to mean a dwelling unit that an innkeeper retains a right of
L40@P1: access to and control of, and that provides or offers all of the following services to all
L41@P1: of the residents:
L42@P1: a) facilities for the safeguarding of personal property, as specified;
L43@P1: b) central telephone service, as specified; and
L44@P1: c) maid, mail, and room services. (Civil Code § 1954.08(b).)
L45@P1: 2) Defines “shelter program” to mean a city, county, continuum of care, state, or
L46@P1: federally funded shelter, interim housing, motel voucher, or emergency shelter
L47@P1: program in which the city, county, federal government entity, or other specified
L48@P1: entity retains an oversight and accountability role in ensuring compliance with
L49@P1: program regulations and proper program administration. (Civ. Code § 1954.08(c).)
L50@P1: 3) Defines “shelter program participant” to mean an occupant of a motel, a hotel, or
L51@P1: other shelter site whose occupancy is solely due to their participation in a shelter
L52@P1: program. (Civ. Code § 1954.08(f).)
L53@P1: 4) Defines “shelter program administrator” to mean a city, county, or continuum of
L54@P1: care entity that retains an oversight role in ensuring compliance with program
L55@P1: regulations and proper program administration. (Civ. Code § 1954.08(d).)
L56@P1: 5) Provides that shelter program participants shall not have their continued occupancy
L57@P1: in a motel, hotel, or a shelter site constitute a new tenancy and shall not be
L58@P1: considered a tenant subject to unlawful detainer proceedings, if the shelter program
L59@P1: meets the following requirements:
L60@P1: a) Adheres to the core components of Housing First;
L61@P1: b) Establishes, adopts, and clearly documents rules governing how and for
L62@P1: what reasons a shelter program participant’s enrollment may be
L63@P1: terminated and the shelter program operator discloses the termination
L64@P1: policy to program participants in writing;
L65@P1: c) Establishes procedures regarding how a shelter program participant will
L66@P1: be provided a written termination notice if a termination occurs, and the
L67@P1: shelter program operator discloses those procedures to shelter program
L68@P1: participants in writing at the commencement of their occupancy;
L69@P1: d) Provides an exit plan upon termination of a shelter program participant
L70@P1: that includes referral to any available local shelter service for which the
L71@P1: participant is eligible, and the shelter program operator makes a good
L72@P1-2: faith, reasonable effort to facilitate an intake, and documents these efforts;AB 2835 (Gabriel)
L73@P2: Page 3 of 10
L74@P2: e) Establishes a grievance process that complies with due process, and the
L75@P2: program operator discloses the grievance process to occupants in writing
L76@P2: at the commencement of their occupancy. (Civ. Code § 1954.09(a).)
L77@P2: 6) Provides that the specified requirements referenced in 5) do not apply to properties
L78@P2: which are being converted from use as a motel or hotel, or from use as a shelter,
L79@P2: interim housing, emergency shelter, or other interim facility to a permanent housing
L80@P2: site from the date that the site receives a certificate of occupancy as a permanent
L81@P2: housing site. (Civ. Code § 1954.09(c).)
L82@P2: 7) Provides that specified building code regulations shall not be interpreted to limit the
L83@P2: length of occupancy for shelter program participants. (Civ. Code § 1954.091(a).)
L84@P2: 8) Emphasizes that the above-described provisions must not be interpreted to confer or
L85@P2: deny any tenants’ rights, and provides that a shelter program participant is entitled
L86@P2: to:
L87@P2: a) continued occupancy in a hotel or motel without creating a tenancy;
L88@P2: b) not to be considered a tenant for purposes of unlawful detainer
L89@P2: proceedings;
L90@P2: c) receipt of a written termination policy;
L91@P2: d) disclosure of the termination procedure;
L92@P2: e) 30 days’ notice prior to termination, except as specified; and
L93@P2: f) the right to appeal termination through a grievance policy, as specified.
L94@P2: (Civ. Code § 1954.091(b).)
L95@P2: 9) Clarifies that a motel or hotel shall not be designated as a nontransient motel or a
L96@P2: nontransient hotel for the California Building Standards Code solely as a result of a
L97@P2: shelter program participant’s occupancy in the motel or hotel beyond a 30-day
L98@P2: period. (Civ. Code § 1954.092(a).)
L99@P2: 10) Prohibits a hotel or motel from doing either of the following:
L100@P2: a) Adopting termination policies specifically for motel or hotel occupants
L101@P2: who are shelter program participants that do not apply to other motel or
L102@P2: hotel occupants who are not participating in a shelter program, impose
L103@P2: restrictions on the ability of program participants to freely enter or exit the
L104@P2: property or access certain areas or amenities of the property that do not
L105@P2: apply to other motel or hotel occupants, or levy charges and fees,
L106@P2: including fees for room card replacements, that do not apply to other
L107@P2: motel or hotel occupants. Specifies that this is a minimum standard for
L108@P2: shelter terminations and that shelter programs may provide greater rights
L109@P2: to participants; and
L110@P2: b) Requiring shelter program participants to check out and reregister, move
L111@P2: out of rooms or between rooms, or from the hotel or motel while actively
L112@P2-3: enrolled in the shelter program unless their continued occupancy of the AB 2835 (Gabriel)
L113@P3: Page 4 of 10
L114@P3: unit of the motel or hotel constitutes a clear and imminent threat to health
L115@P3: and safety of the occupant. (Civ. Code § 1954.092(b).)
L116@P3: 11)Repeals the above-described provisions as of January 1, 2025. (Civ. Code § 1954.093.)
L117@P3: This bill:
L118@P3: 1. Eliminates the sunset provision for the above-described provisions.
L119@P3: 2. Revises the definition of motel or hotel to mean “any hotel, motel, bed and breakfast
L120@P3: inn, or other similar transient lodging establishment.
L121@P3: 3. Provides that a shelter program operator is exempt from providing the required 30-
L122@P3: day notice prior to termination when a shelter program participant has self-exited
L123@P3: from the shelter program.
L124@P3: 4. Specifies that, if a shelter program participant will exit a program due to the
L125@P3: program’s time limits and the participant’s stay is extended for a period that is less
L126@P3: than 30 days, the shelter program administrator or operator may issue an amended
L127@P3: termination notice with an additional period of time equal to the number of days of
L128@P3: the program extension.
L129@P3: 5. Defines “self-exit” as a circumstance where the shelter program participant
L130@P3: voluntarily leaves a shelter program, including for a reason unknown to the shelter
L131@P3: program operator, and does not return to the site or make reasonable contact with
L132@P3: the shelter program operator within 72 hours of leaving. Specifies that the shelter
L133@P3: program operator must contact hospitals, jails, and any other relevant sites to make
L134@P3: a good faith effort to determine the location of the individual and if the exit was
L135@P3: voluntary.
L136@P3: COMMENTS
L137@P3: 1. Author’s statement
L138@P3: According to the author:
L139@P3: In 2022, the legislature passed AB 1991 (Gabriel), which delivered much-needed
L140@P3: clarity and guidance regarding tenancy to motels, hotels, and shelter providers
L141@P3: participating in programs that provide shelter to homeless individuals. Before
L142@P3: the passage of the legislation, shelter programs had to "shuffle" homeless
L143@P3: individuals to new locations every 30 days, an extremely disruptive practice
L144@P3: counterproductive to the goal of assisting this vulnerable community. AB 2835
L145@P3-4: seeks to make these critical changes permanent to ensure service providers, AB 2835 (Gabriel)
L146@P4: Page 5 of 10
L147@P4: motels, hotels, and those experiencing homelessness have a clearly defined set of
L148@P4: protections against arbitrary removal or relocation from shelter programs.
L149@P4: 2. California’s housing crisis and unhoused population
L150@P4: As the cost of housing in California has increased exponentially in recent years, the
L151@P4: number of individuals in the state experiencing homelessness has increased
L152@P4: significantly. In 2023, the United States Housing and Urban Development’s point-intime count of unhoused individuals found 181,399 individuals in California were
L153@P4: experiencing homelessness, which represents a six percent increase from the year
L154@P4: before. 1 A staggering 68 percent of these individuals were unsheltered, meaning they
L155@P4: are currently living outside and not in temporary shelters.2 African Americans are
L156@P4: disproportionately affected by homelessness, as they represented 29 percent of the total
L157@P4: unhoused population in the 2023 count.3
L158@P4: The state’s homelessness crisis is due primarily to the state’s housing crisis, as the state
L159@P4: is experiencing a record shortfall of affordable housing and record high prices for
L160@P4: homes and rent. Data and multiple studies have demonstrated a strong link between
L161@P4: homelessness and the cost of housing.4 The data on the state’s housing crisis also could
L162@P4: not be more clear. It is estimated that the state is experiencing a shortfall of 1,283,734
L163@P4: affordable homes.5 Moreover, 78 percent of extremely low-income households are
L164@P4: severely cost burdened, meaning that they spend more than half of their income on
L165@P4: housing costs, and 52 percent of low-income households are severely cost burdened.6
